source.title: CBSE Senior Secondary School Examination 2025 (XIIth), Chemistry (043), Q.P. Code 56/4/1
source.subject: chemistry
source.notes: Paper prints: Series W4YXZ, 'SET~1' (text layer; stored as SET-1), Q.P. Code 56/4/1, 23 printed pages, 33 questions, Maximum Marks 70, Time allowed 3 hours. Session is not printed on the paper; the marking scheme identifies it as the Senior School Certificate Examination 2024-25 (board exam year 2025). Each page carries bilingual Hindi+English content followed by a pure-English repeat page; question/page numbers reference the pure-English page. Section A (1-16) is MCQ/Assertion-Reason (1 mark); Section B (17-21) very short answer (2 marks); Section C (22-28) short answer (3 marks); Section D (29-30) case-based, with an internal choice in one sub-part of each (4 marks); Section E (31-33) long answer/numerical, each with a full internal-choice alternative (5 marks). Of the 20 PDFs in the question-paper archive, Q.P. codes 56/1/1, 56/1/2, 56/1/3, 56/2/1, 56/2/2 and 56/2/3 are scanned images with no extractable text layer (pdftotext returns only form-feed characters) and were skipped; 56/4/1 is the first code in the archive's listed order with a usable text layer, and its English-medium marking scheme (XII_043_Chemistry_MS_56_4_1.pdf) is present in the marking-scheme archive. The Section A answer table on marking-scheme page 3 renders misaligned in default layout mode; pdftotext -table mode was used to confirm the answer-letter-to-question mapping (1B 2A 3C 4A 5B 6D 7A 8B 9D 10D 11B 12C 13C 14A 15D 16A). The marking scheme is heavy with hand-drawn structures, reaction schemes and multi-line calculations that render as images and are not present in its text layer (flagged per question); where nothing at all was recoverable, officialAnswer is omitted and the gap is noted in extractionIssues. Decimal points print as a middle dot '·' in the question paper's text layer (e.g. '1·28' for '1.28') and were normalized to '.'; degree symbols and standard-electrode-potential superscripts were frequently dropped or split across lines and were reconstructed only where unambiguous (flagged per question).

questions.text:

(ii) Isocyanides are formed when alkyl halides are treated with silver cyanide.
(iii) Methyl chloride reacts faster with OH– ion in SN2 reaction than t-butyl chloride.

questions.text:
Calculate the cell voltage of the voltaic cell which is set up by joining following half-cells at 25°C :
Al / Al3+ (0.001 M) and Ni / Ni2+ (0.1 M)
Given : E°(Ni2+/Ni) = – 0.25 V, E°(Al3+/Al) = – 1.66 V
extractionIssues: Degree symbol reconstructed: '25C' read as '25°C'
Standard-electrode-potential notation rebuilt from a raised 'o' split across lines in the layout ('ENi2+ o / Ni' read as 'E°(Ni2+/Ni)'); check against the PDF
Decimal points printed as a middle dot, normalized to '.'

officialAnswer.text:
2Al + 3Ni2+ → 2Al3+ + 3Ni
E°cell = E°(Ni2+/Ni) – E°(Al3+/Al) ; E°cell = –0.25 – (–1.66) = 1.41 V
n = 6
Ecell = E°cell – (2.303RT/nF) log([Al3+]²/[Ni2+]³)
Ecell = 1.41 – (0.059/6) log([0.001]²/[0.1]³)
Ecell = 1.41 – (0.059/6) log([10]⁻⁶/[10]⁻³)
Ecell = 1.41 – (0.059/6) log 10⁻³
Ecell = 1.41 – (–0.0295)
Ecell = 1.41 + 0.0295
Ecell = 1.439 V / 1.44 V (Deduct ½ mark for no or incorrect unit)

questions.text:
Give explanation for each of the following observations :
(a) With the same d-orbital configuration (d4), Mn3+ ion is an oxidising agent whereas Cr2+ ion is a reducing agent.
(b) Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than that among lanthanoids.
(c) Transition metals form large number of interstitial compounds with H, B, C and N.
extractionIssues: Superscripts flattened: Mn3+, Cr2+

officialAnswer.text:
(a) Change from Mn3+ to Mn2+ results in an extra-stable half-filled d5 configuration. Cr2+ is reducing as its configuration changes from d4 to d3, which is a stable half-filled t2g3 configuration.
(b) Due to poorer shielding offered by 5f electrons than 4f.
(c) H, B, C and N atoms, being small in size, get trapped inside the crystal lattices of transition metals.

questions.text:
According to the generally accepted definition of the ideal solution there are equal interaction forces acting between molecules belonging to the same or different species. (This is equivalent to the statement that the activity of the components equals the concentration.) Strictly speaking, this condition is fulfilled only in exceptional cases for mixtures (optical isomers, isotopic mixtures of an element, hydrocarbon mixtures). It is still usual to talk about ideal solutions as limiting cases in reality since very dilute solutions behave ideally with respect to the solvent. This view is further supported by the fact that Raoult’s law empirically found for describing the behaviour of the solvent in dilute solutions can be deduced thermodynamically via the assumption of ideal behaviour of the solvent.
Answer the following questions :
(a) Give one example of miscible liquid pair which shows negative deviation from Raoult’s law. What is the reason for such deviation ?
(b) (i) State Raoult’s law for a solution containing volatile components.
OR
(b) (ii) Raoult’s law is a special case of Henry’s law. Comment.
(c) Write two characteristics of an ideal solution.

officialAnswer.text:
(a) Chloroform and Acetone (or any other correct example). A–B interactions are stronger than A–A and B–B interactions.
(b)(i) For any solution, the partial vapour pressure of each volatile component is directly proportional to its mole fraction.
OR
(b)(ii) [part of the equation lost in the marking scheme's text layer] When p0 = KH, p is proportional to the mole fraction for both.
(c) The enthalpy of mixing of the pure components in the ideal solution is zero / ΔmixH = 0. The volume of mixing of the pure components in the ideal solution is zero / ΔmixV = 0. (or any other two suitable characteristics)

questions.text:
Ribose and 2-deoxyribose have an important role in biology. Among the most important derivatives are those with phosphate groups attached at the 5 position. Mono-, di- and tri-phosphate forms are important, as well as 3-5 cyclic monophosphates. Purines and pyrimidines form an important class of compounds with ribose and deoxyribose. When these purine and pyrimidine derivatives are coupled to a ribose sugar, they are called nucleosides.
Answer the following questions :
(a) What products would be formed when DNA is hydrolysed ? How is DNA different from RNA with reference to a structure ?
(b) Differentiate between nucleotide and nucleoside.
(c) (i) Mention two important functions of nucleic acid.
OR
(c) (ii) Name the linkage which joins two nucleotides. Name the base that is found in nucleotide of RNA but not in DNA.
extractionIssues: Prime symbols (′) likely lost in extraction: '5 position' may read '5′ position' and '3-5 cyclic' may read '3′-5′ cyclic'; kept as printed since not unambiguous; check against the PDF

officialAnswer.text:
(a) 2-Deoxyribose, Phosphoric acid, Nitrogenous base. DNA: Double stranded helix; RNA: Single stranded helix. (or any other suitable structural difference)
(b) Nucleotide: Pentose sugar + Nitrogenous base + Phosphate. Nucleoside: Pentose sugar + Nitrogenous base.
(c)(i) To preserve genetic information and protein synthesis.
OR
(c)(ii) Phosphodiester linkage. Uracil.

questions.text:
(i) Give reasons :
(I) [Ni(CO)4] is diamagnetic whereas [NiCl4]2– is paramagnetic. [Atomic number : Ni = 28]
(II) CO is a stronger complexing agent than NH3.
(III) The trans isomer of complex [Co(en)2Cl2]+ is optically inactive.
(ii) Using Crystal Field theory, write the number of unpaired electrons in octahedral complexes of Fe3+ in the presence of :
(I) Strong field ligand
(II) Weak field ligand
[Atomic number : Fe = 26]
extractionIssues: Subscripts/superscripts flattened: [Ni(CO)4], [NiCl4]2–, [Co(en)2Cl2]+, Fe3+

officialAnswer.text:
(i)(I) CO, being a strong field ligand, causes pairing of electrons, therefore there is no unpaired electron; Cl– is a weak field ligand, does not cause pairing, therefore presence of unpaired electrons.
(II) CO can form both sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds with the central metal atom / metal-to-ligand bonding creates a synergic effect between CO and the metal.
(III) Mirror images are superimposable / presence of a plane of symmetry.
(ii)(I) ΔO > P, causes pairing of electrons, therefore 1 unpaired electron.
(II) ΔO < P, no pairing of electrons, therefore 5 unpaired electrons.

questions.text:
(i) Name the type of isomerism exhibited by the following compounds. Also draw their corresponding isomers.
(I) [Co(NH3)6] [Cr(CN)6]
(II) [Co(en)3]3+
(III) [Co(NH3)3(NO2)3]
(ii) Differentiate between weak field and strong field ligands. How does the strength of the ligand influence the spin of the complex ?
extractionIssues: Subscripts/superscripts flattened: [Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6], [Co(en)3]3+, [Co(NH3)3(NO2)3]

officialAnswer.text:
(i)(I) Coordination isomerism / [Cr(NH3)6][Co(CN)6].
(II) Optical isomerism; corresponding isomer is a drawn structure — image in the marking scheme, not extracted.
(III) Geometrical isomerism; corresponding isomer is a drawn structure — image in the marking scheme, not extracted.
(ii) Weak field ligands produce a weak field and lead to small splitting of d-orbitals whereas strong field ligands produce a strong field leading to large splitting of d-orbitals. Strong field ligands cause pairing of electrons / a smaller number of unpaired electrons hence produce low spin complexes and weak field ligands cause no pairing of electrons / a greater number of unpaired electrons hence produce high spin complexes.

questions.text:
(i) The initial concentration of N2O5 in the first order reaction :
N2O5 (g) → 2NO2 (g) + 1/2 O2 (g)
was 1.2 × 10⁻² mol L⁻1. The concentration of N2O5 after 60 minutes was 0.2 × 10⁻² mol L⁻1. Calculate the rate constant of the reaction at 318 K.
[log 6 = 0.778]
(ii) Account for the following :
(I) We cannot determine the order of a reaction by taking into consideration the balanced chemical equation.
(II) A bimolecular reaction may become kinetically of first order under a specified condition.
extractionIssues: Subscripts flattened: N2O5, NO2, O2

Notation rebuilt from the PDF layout: a fraction '1 over 2' printed beside O2 read as the coefficient '1/2'; the multiplication sign in '1.2 x 10-2' and superscript exponents were also lost and rebuilt; check against the PDF

officialAnswer.text:
(i) k = (2.303/t) log([R]0/[R])
k = (2.303/60) log(1.2×10⁻²/0.2×10⁻²) = (2.303/60) log 6 = (2.303 × 0.778)/60
k = 2.98 × 10⁻² min⁻1 / 0.0298 min⁻1 (Deduct ½ mark for incorrect or no unit.)
(ii)(I) Order is determined experimentally.
(II) If one of the reactants is taken in excess.

questions.text:
(i) The rate of the chemical reaction doubles for an increase of 10 K in absolute temperature from 298 K. Calculate activation energy (Ea).
[2.303 R = 19.15 J K⁻1 mol⁻1, log 2 = 0.3]
(ii) For a reaction :
2H2O2 –(I–)→ 2H2O + O2
the proposed mechanism is as given below :
(I) H2O2 + I– → H2O + IO– (slow)
(II) H2O2 + IO– → H2O + I– + O2 (fast)
(1) Write rate law for the reaction.
(2) Write the overall order and molecularity of the reaction.
extractionIssues: Subscripts/superscripts flattened: H2O2, H2O, O2, I–, IO–
'I–' printed above the reaction arrow (as a catalyst label) moved inline in parentheses

officialAnswer.text:
(i) log(k2/k1) = (Ea/2.303R)[1/T1 – 1/T2]
log(2k1/k1) = (Ea/19.15)[1/298 – 1/308]
0.3 = Ea[10/(19.15×298×308)]
Ea = (0.3×19.15×298×308)/10
Ea = 52729 J mol⁻1 or 52.729 kJ mol⁻1 (Deduct ½ mark for incorrect or no unit.)
(ii)(1) Rate = k[H2O2][I–]
(2) Overall order : 2 / Second. Molecularity : 2 / Bimolecular.
